L4.explanation: The right framing is per-attempt versus cumulative. A defence with a 1 percent bypass rate fails within a hundred attempts, and attempts are free. Only capability restriction changes the worst case rather than its probability.

L4.prompt_tpl: Explain precisely why parameterised queries solve SQL injection and why no analogous mechanism exists for a {model} today.
L4.answer: A prepared statement is parsed into a plan before any value arrives, so the value travels as a typed parameter and can never become syntax. A transformer has one input channel: instructions and data are tokens in the same sequence, attended over by the same mechanism, with no parse step that fixes the structure before data is supplied. Role markers are conventions the model was trained to weight, not enforced boundaries.
L4.explanation: The distinction is between a mechanism that makes an attack impossible and a training signal that makes it less likely. Everything currently offered for prompt injection is the latter, which is why system design must assume occasional failure.

concepts.t: Indirect prompt injection and the lethal trifecta

L0.body:
INDIRECT injection: the attacker never talks to the model. They plant
instructions in content it will later retrieve: a web page, a PDF, a
calendar invite, an email, a code comment, a filename. Greshake et
al., 2023, demonstrated this against production applications.

Willison's LETHAL TRIFECTA. A system is exploitable when all hold:
  1 access to private data
  2 exposure to untrusted content
  3 the ability to communicate externally

Any two are survivable. Cut one leg deterministically. Note that
markdown image rendering is an exfiltration channel.
L0.cloze:
Indirect prompt injection plants instructions in content the model {{c1::retrieves}} rather than in what the user types.
The lethal trifecta is private data access, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to {{c2::exfiltrate}}; a system is exploitable only when all {{c3::three}} are present.
Rendering a model-composed {{c4::image}} URL is an exfiltration channel, because the client fetches it automatically.

concepts.L1: The high-impact form of prompt injection: instructions arrive through retrieved content rather than user input, so the victim never sees them and the attacker never needs access to the application.
concepts.L2: The exfiltration leg is the one teams forget, because it does not look like a tool. Rendering markdown images, following links, or any client-side fetch of a model-composed URL is an outbound channel with no confirmation step.
concepts.L3: The trifecta framing makes the security question tractable. Rather than asking whether the model can be fooled, which it can, ask which of the three legs your architecture actually requires, and remove one deterministically. Removing untrusted content is rarely possible for a retrieval or agent product. Removing private data from scope works for some sessions. Removing egress is usually the achievable one, and it must be enforced outside the model: strip or refuse to render model-composed URLs, allowlist outbound destinations at the network layer, and require human confirmation for anything that sends data outward. Each is deterministic, which is what model-based defences lack.

L4.prompt_tpl: An assistant reads the user's {private} and can browse the web and render markdown. Identify the trifecta legs and the cheapest deterministic mitigation.
L4.answer: Private data: the user's own content. Untrusted content: fetched web pages. Exfiltration: browsing plus markdown image rendering, both of which issue outbound requests to attacker-chosen URLs. Cheapest deterministic cut: disable rendering of model-composed URLs and images, and route any outbound fetch through an allowlist, so no attacker-chosen destination is reachable.
L4.explanation: Cutting egress is usually cheapest because it does not degrade the product's core value, whereas removing retrieval or private data does. The requirement is that the cut is enforced by the client and network, not by asking the model to refrain.

L4.prompt_tpl: A code-review agent reads pull requests from external contributors and has a tool that can post comments and one that can read {scope}. What is the attack, and what is the design fix?
L4.answer: An external contributor puts instructions in a diff or a code comment; the agent retrieves them, and can be directed to read the private scope and encode it into a public comment, which is the exfiltration channel. Fix: run the agent on untrusted pull requests with no access to private scopes at all, and require that any posted output be reviewed, or split into two agents that never share a session.
L4.explanation: This is the trifecta with a non-obvious exfiltration leg: a comment on a public pull request is an outbound channel. Any tool that writes somewhere the attacker can read counts as egress.

L0.body:
Different attacker, different victim, different fix.

  JAILBREAK  the USER attacks, wanting output the provider's policy
             forbids. The victim is the policy. Defence: alignment
             training, input/output classifiers, refusal.
  INJECTION  a THIRD PARTY attacks; the user is the victim, and the
             attacker's text arrives through retrieved data.
             Defence: capability restriction outside the model.

A model that never emits disallowed content can still be directed to
exfiltrate a user's data: a tool call is not disallowed.
L0.cloze:
In a {{c1::jailbreak}} the user is the attacker and the provider's policy is the victim; in prompt injection a {{c2::third party}} is the attacker and the user is the victim.
Jailbreak defences are alignment and {{c3::classifiers}}; injection defences are {{c4::capability}} restrictions in the surrounding system.
Robustness to one does not imply robustness to the other.

concepts.L1: Two attacks that both involve adversarial text and are otherwise unrelated. They differ in who the attacker is, who is harmed, and consequently in what mitigations apply.
concepts.L2: The confusion has a concrete cost: teams cite jailbreak-resistance evaluations as evidence that an agent is safe to give tools to. Exfiltrating a user's data through a tool call is not policy-violating content, so no content classifier will flag it.
concepts.L3: The distinction determines where the boundary sits. For jailbreaks, provider and application are on the same side and the user is adversarial, so the defence can live inside the model and its filters, and a residual failure rate is a policy problem rather than a compromise of a specific user. For injection the user and provider are on the same side and the adversary is outside both, so the defence must constrain actions rather than words, and a residual failure rate is a direct compromise of that user's data. A single evaluation number covering both is meaningless: a model's refusal behaviour says nothing about whether an agent with credentials can be redirected.

L4.prompt_tpl: A vendor reports a {pct} reduction in successful jailbreaks in the latest model. Your team wants to use this to justify giving an agent write access to production systems. Respond.
L4.answer: The metric measures refusal of policy-violating content when the user is adversarial. Giving an agent write access is exposed to prompt injection, where a third party's text redirects a permitted action, and a tool call is not policy-violating output. The relevant evidence would be injection-specific evaluations plus, more importantly, an architecture where a redirected agent cannot cause unbounded harm.
L4.explanation: The general rule for evaluating any AI security claim is to check whether the benchmark's threat model matches yours. Here the attacker, the victim and the harmful output are all different, so the number does not transfer.

L4.prompt_tpl: For a {system}, state who the attacker is, who the victim is, and which defence layer applies, under each of jailbreaking and prompt injection.
L4.answer: Jailbreak: the end user is the attacker, the provider's policy is the victim, and the defence is model alignment plus input and output classifiers. Injection: a third party who authored retrieved content is the attacker, the end user is the victim, and the defence is capability restriction, egress control and confirmation gates in the application around the model.
L4.explanation: Writing the two rows out explicitly is the exercise. Most confused designs become obvious once the attacker and victim columns are filled in, because the defences land in visibly different layers.

L0.body:
Poisoning attacks the model before it exists.

  AVAILABILITY  degrade overall accuracy
  TARGETED      change the prediction on specific inputs
  BACKDOOR      train an association between a TRIGGER and an
                attacker-chosen output. Clean accuracy is unchanged,
                so ordinary evaluation cannot detect it.

Carlini et al., 2023: SPLIT-VIEW (content at indexed URLs changes
after collection) and FRONTRUNNING (inject just before a Wikipedia
snapshot, revert after). ~60 USD to poison 0.01% of LAION-400M.

Defence: pin datasets by CONTENT HASH, not URL. Sign snapshots.
L0.cloze:
A {{c1::backdoor}} associates a trigger with an attacker-chosen output while leaving clean-data accuracy unchanged, so standard evaluation does not detect it.
{{c2::Split-view}} poisoning exploits the fact that web-scale datasets store {{c3::URLs}} rather than content, and frontrunning exploits periodic snapshots.
The defence is to pin data by content {{c4::hash}} and sign snapshots.

concepts.L1: Manipulating training data so the resulting model behaves as the attacker intends. Backdoors are the dangerous form because they leave benign-input accuracy intact and activate only on a trigger the attacker controls.
concepts.L2: The obstacle is not the fraction of data required, which is tiny, but the belief that an attacker cannot influence a web-scale corpus. Datasets distributed as URL lists let an attacker change the content after collection, which requires no access to the dataset at all.
concepts.L3: Backdoors are hard to detect because the model is correct on everything the evaluator will think to test. The trigger is chosen by the attacker and can be arbitrarily specific, so the search space for detection is the input space itself. That makes provenance the practical control rather than testing. Pinning by content hash removes split-view poisoning entirely, because the downloader either gets the bytes the annotator saw or gets nothing; signed snapshots address frontrunning by making contents attributable after the fact. For any security-relevant model, prefer a curated corpus you can enumerate, and keep an evaluation set whose provenance you control end to end.

L4.prompt_tpl: Poisoning 0.01 percent of a {n}-example dataset. How many examples is that, and why does the number make URL-based distribution the weak link?
L4.answer: 0.01 percent of 400 million is 40000 examples, and of 700 million is 70000. Buying expired domains that appear in such an index and serving different content is enough to control that many entries, which is why the estimated cost was about 60 US dollars rather than anything requiring dataset access.
L4.explanation: The counterintuitive part is that the absolute count is large while the cost is trivial, because a single expired domain can account for many thousands of index entries. Distribution by reference rather than by content is what makes the economics work for the attacker.

L4.prompt_tpl: You fine-tune a {model} on a scraped corpus for a security-relevant classification task. Which control most reduces backdoor risk?
L4.answer: Pin every training example by content hash and use a curated corpus whose provenance you can enumerate.
L4.explanation: Backdoors preserve clean-data accuracy, so a larger validation set finds nothing. Differential privacy limits memorisation of individual examples but does not prevent a trigger association learned from many poisoned examples. Controlling what enters training is the only control that acts before the association is learned.
options: Pin every training example by content hash and use a curated corpus whose provenance you can enumerate.
Hold out a larger validation set and require high accuracy on it.
Train with differential privacy so no single example influences the model.

L0.body:
Two distinct threats to a model as an asset.

EXTRACTION via the API. Carlini et al., 2024, "Stealing Part of a
Production Language Model": black-box querying recovered the embedding
projection layer of production models, including hidden dimensions of
gpt-3.5-turbo, for under 20 USD on smaller ones. Logit or logprob
access makes it cheap.
  Defence: no full logit vectors, restrict logit_bias, rate limit per
  principal, treat high-volume programmatic access as a signal.

EXFILTRATION of the weights is an insider and access-control problem:
least privilege, key custody, egress monitoring.
L0.cloze:
Model extraction through an API is made efficient by the precision of what the API returns per query, above all full {{c1::logit}} vectors.
Carlini et al. recovered the {{c2::embedding projection}} layer of production models, revealing hidden dimensions, for on the order of thousands of dollars.
Weight {{c3::exfiltration}} is an ordinary access-control and {{c4::insider}} problem, defended with least privilege and egress monitoring.

concepts.L1: Two ways an adversary obtains model capability: reconstructing part of it from query responses, or copying the weight files. They have entirely different controls and are routinely conflated.
concepts.L2: Extraction cost scales with information returned per query, not with model size. An API that returns full log-probability vectors is far cheaper to extract from than one returning only sampled text, which makes it a product decision with a security consequence.
concepts.L3: The extraction result matters because it disproved the assumption that a black-box API leaks nothing structural. The attack exploits the fact that outputs lie in a subspace whose dimension equals the model's hidden size, so enough queries reveal that dimension and then the projection itself, for hundreds or thousands of dollars rather than the cost of training. That layer is not the whole model, but it establishes that API surfaces leak in proportion to output precision. Exfiltration deserves the opposite framing: nothing about it is novel. Enumerate every copy of the weights, minimise that number, and alert on egress volume.

L4.prompt_tpl: Your inference API currently returns full log-probabilities for the top {k} tokens. A team asks to expose all of them for research use. What is the security tradeoff?
L4.answer: Returning full logit vectors reduces the number of queries needed for extraction by orders of magnitude, because each response constrains the output subspace far more tightly. If exposed, gate it behind a separate authenticated tier with per-principal rate limits, volume alerting, and contractual terms, rather than making it a default of the public API.
L4.explanation: The tradeoff is between research utility and extraction cost, and it is continuous rather than binary. The design lever is how much information leaves per query and to whom, which is why a separate tier with identity and quotas is the usual resolution.

L4.prompt_tpl: Distinguish the controls for model extraction and for weight exfiltration in an organisation with {n} engineers, and explain why one is an ML problem and the other is not.
L4.answer: Extraction is an API design and abuse-detection problem: limit output precision, rate limit per authenticated principal, and detect programmatic query patterns. Exfiltration is a classic insider and access-control problem: minimise the number of weight copies, use hardware-backed key custody, apply two-person rules to exports, and monitor egress volume. Only the first depends on anything about machine learning.
L4.explanation: The reason to separate them is that conflating the two produces the wrong roadmap: teams add rate limits and believe they have addressed weight theft, when the relevant question is how many people and processes can read the file.

prereqs: Least privilege and the Saltzer-Schroeder principles

L0.body:
Two privacy attacks on a trained model.

MEMBERSHIP INFERENCE (Shokri et al., 2017): given a candidate record
and query access, decide whether it was in the training set. The
signal is confidence. For a medical model, membership is the
sensitive fact.

EXTRACTION: recover data verbatim. Nasr, Carlini et al., 2023, used a
DIVERGENCE attack against an aligned chat model and recovered training
data at ~150x the normal rate. Alignment hides memorisation.

Defences: deduplicate training data (cheapest and most effective),
differential privacy, output filtering, logprob and rate limits.
L0.cloze:
Membership inference decides whether a record was in the {{c1::training set}}, and its signal is the model's higher {{c2::confidence}} on memorised data.
The divergence attack recovered training data from an aligned model at about {{c3::150}} times the normal rate, showing that alignment {{c4::hides}} memorisation rather than removing it.
The cheapest effective defence is training-data {{c5::deduplication}}.

concepts.L1: Two attacks that treat a model as a lossy database of its training set. One asks whether a record was present; the other recovers records verbatim.
concepts.L2: Alignment training is often mistaken for a privacy control. It changes the model's default behaviour, not what it stored, so prompts that push the model off its aligned distribution recover memorised text that ordinary interaction never surfaces.
concepts.L3: Memorisation is a consequence of capacity and duplication, and duplication is the lever you control. Sequences repeated many times in a corpus are memorised far more readily than unique ones, so aggressive deduplication reduces extractable content substantially at no utility cost, which is why it is the first recommendation rather than the last. Differential privacy provides an actual bound on any single example's influence and therefore on membership inference, but the noise costs accuracy. The divergence result generalises: any memorisation evaluation run only on in-distribution prompts underestimates it, because the attacker need not stay in distribution.

L4.prompt_tpl: A model is fine-tuned on {data} and the team argues that alignment refusals prevent it from revealing them. Explain why this reasoning fails and what would actually reduce the risk.
L4.answer: Refusal behaviour is a learned default over the aligned distribution, not a property of what the weights encode, so prompts that push the model off that distribution can surface memorised text. What reduces risk: deduplicate and redact the corpus before training, apply differential privacy if the utility cost is acceptable, filter outputs against known sensitive patterns, and restrict logprob access and query volume.
L4.explanation: The distinction between what a model knows and what it will say by default is the whole point. Security controls must act on the first, because the second is a behavioural tendency an adversary can steer.

L4.prompt_tpl: You must reduce membership-inference risk for a model trained on {n} sensitive records with minimal accuracy loss. Which control first?
L4.answer: Deduplicate the training corpus and reduce the number of epochs over rare records, then restrict confidence outputs.
L4.explanation: Membership inference reads a confidence gap between seen and unseen data, which is widened by repeated exposure to individual records. Deduplication and fewer epochs narrow that gap at essentially no utility cost. Differential privacy bounds it rigorously but costs accuracy, so it is the second step, not the first.
options: Deduplicate the training corpus and reduce the number of epochs over rare records, then restrict confidence outputs.
Train with a strict differential privacy budget from the outset.
Add a refusal classifier that blocks questions about the training data.

L0.body:
A small, deliberately chosen perturbation that changes a prediction
while leaving the input perceptually unchanged: minimise a norm of
delta subject to f(x + delta) != f(x), under an $L_{\infty}$ bound.

FGSM (Goodfellow et al., 2014) steps along the sign of the loss
gradient; PGD iterates inside the norm ball; Carlini-Wagner broke a
long list of published defences.

  TRANSFERABILITY  an example crafted on one model often fools another
  GRADIENT MASKING most defences make gradients uninformative rather
                   than the model robust
L0.cloze:
An adversarial example is a perturbation within a norm bound, typically {{c1::L-infinity}}, that changes the prediction while leaving the input perceptually unchanged.
{{c2::Transferability}} means an example crafted on one model often fools another, so the attacker does not need white-box access.
Most proposed defences fail through {{c3::gradient masking}}, and {{c4::adversarial training}} is the main one that survives, at a cost in accuracy and training time.

concepts.L1: Inputs perturbed by a small, deliberately chosen amount that change a model's output. They are a property of how high-dimensional decision boundaries are learned, not a bug in a particular architecture.
concepts.L2: Almost every published defence has been broken, usually because it obscured gradients rather than moving the decision boundary. A defence evaluated only against the attacks it was designed to stop tells you nothing.
concepts.L3: Gradient masking is the pattern worth internalising because it recurs. A defence adds a non-differentiable step, randomisation, or a saturating transform; gradient-based attacks then fail, the paper reports high robust accuracy, and an adaptive attacker who estimates gradients differently restores the original success rate. Robustness must therefore be evaluated against attacks constructed with full knowledge of the defence, the standard cryptography adopted long ago. Transferability makes the threat practical, since an attacker without your weights can craft examples on a surrogate. For deployed systems the useful controls are rate limiting and a human decision on consequential outcomes.

L4.prompt_tpl: A paper reports {acc} percent robust accuracy for a defence that quantises inputs before classification, evaluated against FGSM and PGD. What is the likely methodological flaw?
L4.answer: Quantisation is non-differentiable, so gradients through it are uninformative and gradient-based attacks fail for reasons unrelated to robustness. This is gradient masking. A correct evaluation uses an adaptive attack, for instance a differentiable approximation of the quantiser via a straight-through estimator, or a gradient-free attack, and would likely show robust accuracy collapsing.
L4.explanation: The tell is that the defence introduces a non-differentiable or randomised component and is evaluated only with gradient-based attacks. This pattern has accounted for the large majority of broken defences.

L4.prompt_tpl: You deploy a vision model for {task} and cannot afford adversarial training. What system-level controls reduce risk?
L4.answer: Combine the model with independent non-model signals so a single fooled prediction is not decisive, rate limit per principal so an attacker cannot search for a working perturbation online, log and review low-confidence and near-boundary cases, and keep a human decision on high-consequence outcomes. Detecting query patterns consistent with perturbation search is also cheap.
L4.explanation: The framing is to treat the model as one unreliable sensor rather than as an oracle. Most deployed harm comes from a single model output being authoritative, which is an architecture choice rather than a model property.

concepts.t: Agent security, tool use and the inference endpoint

L0.body:
An agent is a confused deputy with credentials and a loop. Design for
instructions chosen by an attacker.

Capability layer, enforced OUTSIDE the model:
  - scope every tool credential minimally, per session, short-lived
  - separate read from write; require human confirmation for anything
    irreversible, outbound, or costly
  - allowlist egress destinations at the network layer
  - never let the model choose which credential to use
  - budget the loop: cap steps, tool calls, tokens, wall time

Model output is untrusted input to whatever consumes it next.
L0.cloze:
An agent should be designed on the assumption that its instructions may have been chosen by an {{c1::attacker}}, so tool credentials are scoped per session and the model never chooses which {{c2::credential}} to use.
Actions that are irreversible or send data outward require human {{c3::confirmation}}.
Model output must be treated as {{c4::untrusted input}} to whatever consumes it next, never reflected into a shell, a template or a query.

concepts.L1: The security design for systems where a model chooses actions. The controls are conventional authorisation and rate limiting, applied at the boundary between the model's output and the effects it can cause.
concepts.L2: The commonly missed rule is that model output is untrusted input downstream. Teams sanitise what goes into the model and then interpolate its output into a shell command or a template, which turns any injection into ordinary command or template injection.
concepts.L3: Framing an agent as a confused deputy makes the design tractable, because the confused-deputy fix is known: bind authority to the request rather than to the process. Concretely, the credential handed to a tool call is derived from the user's entitlement for that specific action, is short-lived, and cannot be broadened by anything the model emits. Step and cost budgets matter for a second reason beyond runaway loops: they bound how many attempts an injected instruction gets. On the endpoint the risks are conventional but the cost asymmetry is not, since one very long context can consume orders of magnitude more compute, making per-principal token quotas the correct limit.

L4.prompt_tpl: An agent's output is passed to a shell for a {task}, after the team added an input filter for prompt injection. Name the flaw and the correct boundary.
L4.answer: Model output is being treated as trusted. Any successful injection, and injection has no reliable filter, becomes shell command injection with the agent's privileges. The correct boundary is to never pass model output to a shell: expose a fixed set of parameterised operations the model selects by name, with arguments validated against types and allowlists, executed without a shell.
L4.explanation: This is the same lesson as parameterised queries, one layer out. The model chooses which operation to run from a closed set; it never composes the command. That makes a successful injection bounded by the set you defined.

L4.prompt_tpl: You are setting quotas on an inference endpoint used by {n} tenants. Which limit is the right primary control?
L4.answer: A per-principal token budget over a time window, plus a hard concurrency cap and a maximum context length.
L4.explanation: Cost is roughly proportional to tokens processed and generated, not to request count, so a request-rate limit lets one tenant with very long contexts consume the capacity of thousands. Token budgets bound the actual resource, concurrency caps bound tail latency, and a context length cap bounds the worst single request.
options: A per-principal token budget over a time window, plus a hard concurrency cap and a maximum context length.
A per-IP request rate limit of a few hundred requests per minute.
A global request rate limit sized to the cluster's peak throughput.

concepts.t: Logging and detection that is actually useful

L0.body:
Log what an investigator needs, with joinable fields, and nothing
that makes the log a liability.

  Log:    authentication success AND failure, with the principal
          authorisation denials (a spike signals enumeration)
          privilege changes, credential creation, admin actions
          every tool call an automated system makes
  Fields: timestamp, actor id, source address, request id, target
          object id, outcome, denial reason
  Never:  passwords, tokens, session ids, card numbers

CORRELATION: one request id across services.
INTEGRITY: append-only, off-host, 90 days.
L0.cloze:
Useful logs carry an actor id, a {{c1::request id}} propagated across services, a target object id and an {{c2::outcome}}, so one identifier reconstructs a request path.
Logs must never contain passwords, tokens or {{c3::session ids}}, because that makes the log store a credential store.
A09:2025 was renamed to Alerting because a log with no {{c4::owner}} and no runbook is not a control.

concepts.L1: Logging for investigation rather than for debugging. The test is whether a specific past question can be answered from the log alone, months later, by someone who did not write the code.
concepts.L2: The common failure is volume without joinability. Terabytes of unstructured application logs with no propagated request identifier and no actor field cannot answer the only question that matters during an incident, which is what one principal did across services.
concepts.L3: Retention is chosen by dwell time, not by cost tolerance. Intrusions are routinely discovered weeks or months after initial access, so a 30-day window frequently means the relevant events are already gone when the investigation starts, which is why 90 days is a floor and a year is common for authentication and administrative events. Integrity matters for the same reason: an attacker with host access will edit or delete local logs, so shipping off-host to an append-only store is what preserves evidence. On alerting, each alert needs a named owner, an expected volume and a runbook, and alerts firing without action should be deleted rather than tolerated.

L4.prompt_tpl: An incident is reported {t} after the initial access. Your logs retain 30 days at debug verbosity with no request id. What can and cannot be reconstructed?
L4.answer: The initial access is outside retention, so the entry point cannot be established. Without a propagated request id you cannot follow one actor's path across services, so lateral movement is guesswork. You can at best describe recent activity. Fix ordering: propagate a request id and log an actor field, extend retention on authentication and administrative events to at least a year, and reduce verbosity elsewhere to pay for it.
L4.explanation: The tradeoff is verbosity against retention at a fixed budget. Security value is concentrated in a small number of event types, so keeping those far longer and everything else far shorter is strictly better than uniform retention.

L4.prompt_tpl: A team logs the full request body on {endpoint} to aid debugging, in a store readable by all engineers. Name the risk and the correct change.
L4.answer: The log becomes a credential store: passwords, tokens and session identifiers are captured in plaintext and are readable far more widely than the systems they authenticate to. Correct change: redact known-sensitive fields at the emitting library rather than downstream, never log bodies on authentication endpoints, and restrict the log store to the same access level as the data it may contain.
L4.explanation: Redacting at the emitter rather than in the pipeline is the important detail. A downstream redaction rule fails open on any field name nobody anticipated, and the raw value has already been written and replicated by then.

L0.body:
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3 (April 2025) reframes incident response as a
CSF 2.0 community profile, not a linear four-phase lifecycle.

Decide in advance:
  who declares an incident, and who can page whom
  containment vs evidence: pulling the host destroys memory forensics
  when to rotate credentials, and what exactly rotates
  who talks to customers, regulators and press, on what clock
  a written timeline kept as you go

Disclosure: Project Zero's 90 days is the de facto norm. Publish a
security.txt, promise not to pursue good-faith researchers, respond
within days, issue a CVE.
L0.cloze:
NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3, published April 2025, restructures incident response as a {{c1::CSF 2.0}} community profile rather than a linear lifecycle.
The containment decision trades speed against {{c2::evidence}}, since powering off a host destroys volatile memory.
{{c3::Coordinated}} disclosure gives a vendor a fixed window, conventionally {{c4::90}} days, and {{c5::CVSS}} scores severity in the abstract rather than in your environment.

concepts.L1: The organisational half of security: deciding in advance who does what during an incident, and how externally reported vulnerabilities are received and fixed. Both are process controls whose value is entirely in having decided beforehand.
concepts.L2: CVSS is routinely used as a patch-priority queue, which it is not. A base score ignores whether the component is reachable, whether it holds data, and whether an exploit exists, so a 9.8 on an internal service can matter less than a 6.5 on the login path.
concepts.L3: The containment tradeoff most often goes wrong in the first hour. Pulling power stops the attacker and destroys volatile evidence including process memory, network connections and encryption keys, which may be the only record of what was taken; isolating at the network layer preserves that state at the cost of leaving the process running. The decision depends on whether you most need to stop damage or to know its extent, and it should be made by a named role rather than improvised. On disclosure, a published contact and a good-faith commitment materially change reporter behaviour: researchers who cannot find a contact publish anyway.

L4.prompt_tpl: You detect an active intrusion on a host holding {data}. The attacker appears still connected. What is the containment decision and why?
L4.answer: Isolate the host at the network layer while leaving it running, then capture memory before any shutdown.
L4.explanation: Network isolation stops ongoing exfiltration and lateral movement immediately while preserving process memory, open connections and in-memory keys, which are often the only evidence of what was accessed. Powering off destroys that. Watching without isolating trades certain further loss for marginal intelligence.
options: Isolate the host at the network layer while leaving it running, then capture memory before any shutdown.
Power off the host immediately to stop the attacker.
Leave the host connected and monitor to learn the attacker's objectives.

L4.prompt_tpl: A researcher reports a vulnerability and sets a {days}-day deadline. Your fix requires a coordinated release with a downstream vendor. How do you handle it?
L4.answer: Acknowledge within days, confirm the finding, and state a concrete remediation date with reasoning rather than asking for open-ended delay. Loop the downstream vendor in early under the same clock. If the date will slip, say so before the deadline with a revised date; deadlines are usually extended for demonstrated progress and rarely for silence. Publish an advisory and a CVE at release.
L4.explanation: Researchers extend deadlines for communication and evidence of work, not for requests. The failure mode that produces early publication is silence, so the operational rule is to respond quickly even when you cannot fix quickly.

prereqs: Logging and detection that is actually useful
